Vacancy-engineered g-C₃N₄
Defect engineering offers a rational strategy to tailor the electronic structure and interfacial charge 
storage of graphitic carbon nitride (g-C₃N₄) for electrochemical energy storage. Here, we present a 
first-principles study of nitrogen edge vacancies in both triazine-based (g-C₂₇N₃₆) and heptazine-
based (h-g-C₂₄N₃₂) frameworks, systematically correlating vacancy concentration with electronic 
structure evolution and quantum capacitance (Cq). Spin-polarized DFT calculations reveal that 
increasing N-vacancy concentration induces lattice contraction, Fermi level shifts, charge 
redistribution, and progressive bandgap narrowing. In the triazine system, vacancy levels beyond 
~8% drive a semiconductor-to-metal transition due to defect states emerging near the Fermi level, 
significantly enhancing the density of states (DOS). This leads to a substantial rise in Cq, reaching 
125.18 μF cm⁻² for C₂₇N₂₈—nearly two orders of magnitude higher than pristine g-C₃N₄. Q–V 
analysis further indicates asymmetric charge storage behavior, suggesting distinct operating 
windows for positive and negative electrodes. By contrast, the heptazine framework exhibits more 
gradual electronic modulation, with band-gap reduction toward near-semi-metallic behavior at 
moderate vacancy levels. The optimal C₂₄N₃₀ configuration achieves a peak Cq of 109.89 μF cm⁻², 
attributed to vacancy-induced mid-gap states and enhanced electronic compressibility. While 
triazine structures deliver higher peak capacitance, heptazine systems show comparatively lower 
defect formation energies, indicating better thermodynamic feasibility. Overall, this work 
establishes a clear structure–electronic–capacitance relationship in vacancy-engineered g-C₃N₄ and 
identifies an optimal defect regime that maximizes quantum capacitance without compromising 
structural stability, providing atomistic design insights for next-generation supercapacitor

4. Final Summary

In this work, we established a comprehensive structure–electronic–capacitance correlation in vacancy-
engineered graphitic carbon nitride through systematic first-principles investigations of nitrogen edge
vacancies in both triazine-based (g-C₂₇N₃₆) and heptazine-based (h-g-C₂₄N₃₂) frameworks. Spin-polarized
DFT calculations reveal that controlled N-vacancy introduction induces lattice contraction, charge
redistribution, Fermi level shifts, and progressive band-gap narrowing, fundamentally altering the
electronic compressibility of the system.
Vacancy engineering generates mid-gap states near the Fermi level, leading to enhanced density of
states (DOS) and a transition toward quasi-metallic behavior. In the triazine framework, vacancy
concentrations beyond ~8% trigger a semiconductor-to-metal transition due to defect-state
delocalization, producing a pronounced enhancement in quantum capacitance. The C₂₇N₂₈ confi guration
achieves a maximum Cq of 125.18 μF cm⁻²—nearly two orders of magnitude higher than pristine g-C₃N₄
—accompanied by asymmetric Q–V characteristics that suggest distinct positive and negative electrode
operating windows. However, excessive vacancy formation broadens mid-gap states, limits effective
charge accumulation, and destabilizes the N-bridged lattice backbone.
In contrast, the heptazine framework exhibits a more gradual electronic modulation under increasing
vacancy concentration. Moderate N-vacancy incorporation induces near-semi-metallic behavior without
abrupt structural destabilization. The optimal C₂₄N₃₀ configuration delivers a peak Cq of 109.89 μF cm⁻²,
arising from vacancy-induced mid-gap states and enhanced electronic compressibility. Importantly,
lower defect formation energies in the heptazine system indicate greater thermodynamic feasibility
compared to the triazine counterpart. At low vacancy concentrations, heptazine-nitride demonstrates
superior electrochemical stability while maintaining significantly improved capacitance over the pristine
structure.
Overall, our results identify an optimal defect regime that maximizes quantum capacitance while
preserving structural integrity. Although triazine systems provide higher peak capacitance at elevated
vacancy levels, low-vacancy heptazine nitride emerges as the most balanced and practically viable
candidate for metal-free supercapacitor electrodes. These insights provide atomistic design guidelines
for tailoring the capacitive performance of graphitic carbon nitride through rational defect engineering
and may assist experimental efforts in developing next-generation sustainable energy storage
materials.

In QuantumATK (ATK-VNL), the mesh cutoff and SCF convergence criteria are defined in the
calculator (DFT) settings. Here’s how you can obtain and report them:
 1. Mesh Cutoff (e.g., 75 Ha)
How to check/set:
1. Open your configuration in Builder.
2. Go to Add → Calculator → DFT (LCAO or Plane Wave).
3. In the Numerical Accuracy section:
Find Density Mesh Cutoff.
Set or read the value (e.g., 75 Hartree).
 This corresponds directly to the mesh cutoff energy used for real-space grid integration.
 2. Convergence Criteria (RMS Density Matrix & Total Energy)
How to check:
1. In the same DFT Calculator window,
2. Go to the Self-Consistent Field (SCF) settings.
3. Look for:
Density Matrix Convergence Tolerance (this is your RMS density matrix criterion)
Energy Convergence Tolerance (total energy criterion)

Typical reported values are:
RMS density matrix: ~10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁶
Energy convergence: ~10⁻⁵ eV
 3. If Calculation Is Already Finished
You can extract the exact values from:
Script Generator (check the Python script used)
Or open the .log file in the Job Manager and search for:
density_mesh_cutoff
density_matrix_tolerance
energy_tolerance
 Example (Python Script in ATK)
Python
calculator = LCAOCalculator(
    basis_set=...,
    density_mesh_cutoff=75*Hartree,
    iteration_control_parameters=IterationControlParameters(
        density_matrix_tolerance=1e-5,
        energy_tolerance=1e-5*eV
    )
)

Systematic Creation of Nitrogen Vacancies in Triazine g-C₂₇N₃₆
Nitrogen vacancies were introduced systematically into the optimized triazine-based g-C₂₇N₃₆ supercell
to investigate the effect of defect concentration on the electronic structure and quantum capacitance.

The pristine configuration (C₂₇N₃₆) was first fully relaxed using spin-polarized DFT until the forces and
total energy were converged.
Vacancies were then generated by selectively removing edge nitrogen atoms from the triazine units
while preserving the overall lattice symmetry as much as possible. Edge nitrogen sites were
preferentially chosen because they possess lower coordination numbers compared to bridging nitrogen
atoms and therefore exhibit lower defect formation energies, making them thermodynamically more
favorable.
The vacancy concentration was increased stepwise as follows:
C₂₇N₃₆ → C₂₇N₃₃ (1 N vacancy, ~8.3%)
C₂₇N₃₆ → C₂₇N₃₀ (2 N vacancies, ~16.7%)
C₂₇N₃₆ → C₂₇N₂₈ (3 N vacancies, ~22.2%)
C₂₇N₃₆ → C₂₇N₂₆ (4 N vacancies, ~27.8%)
C₂₇N₃₆ → C₂₇N₂₅ (5 N vacancies, ~30.6%)
At each defect level, the structure was fully re-optimized to allow local bond reconstruction and lattice
relaxation around the vacancy site. Care was taken to distribute multiple vacancies as far apart as
possible within the supercell to minimize artificial vacancy–vacancy interactions arising from periodic
boundary conditions.
This controlled, stepwise removal of nitrogen atoms enabled a systematic evaluation of how increasing
vacancy concentration influences lattice distortion, defect-state formation, bandgap evolution, density
of states near the Fermi level, and consequently quantum capacitance.
